cues.text: A Church Robbed
On February 24, 1772, unknown thieves broke into the church of St. Peter in Patierno, near Naples, Italy, and made off with a number of consecrated Hosts along with other valuables.
No trace of them turned up for a full month despite the parish's efforts to locate what had been taken.
Buried Beneath Manure
A month after the theft, mysterious lights were reported at night on land belonging to the Duke of Grottolelle, along with the repeated appearance of a dove hovering over one particular spot by day.
Investigating the site, searchers found the stolen Hosts buried beneath a pile of manure — and, despite this thoroughly unpromising place of concealment, completely intact.
Matched to the Church of Origin
The recovered Hosts were confirmed to have come specifically from St. Peter's in Patierno.
Their exact circumference matched the flat-iron mold the parish used to produce its own Hosts.

Each still bore an engraved mark identifying it as the property of that particular church—physical evidence tying the discovery directly back to the original theft rather than leaving it a matter of assumption.
A Two-Year Formal Inquiry
Vicar General Monsignor Onorati oversaw a formal diocesan process examining the event.
It ran for two full years, from 1772 to 1774, gathering testimony from several prominent scientists of the day.
Among them was Dr. Domenico Cotugno of the Royal University of Naples.

Their collective conclusion held that the Hosts' preservation could not be explained by ordinary physical processes and exceeded the powers of natural causes — a judgment the archbishop's curia formally endorsed on August 29, 1774.
St. Alphonsus Maria de Liguori, already associated with the Scala account four decades earlier, described the Patierno event in his own writings as well.
Legacy
The devotion continued at Patierno for two centuries, reinforced by a diocesan Eucharistic Year declared in 1971.
In 1978, however, the relic itself — the recovered Hosts of 1772 — was stolen once again, this time never to be recovered.
The parish was left with the documented record of the event, but not the physical object at its center.

What survives is the two-year formal inquiry and its scientific testimony — an unusually thorough paper trail for an eighteenth-century account, even after the relic it describes was ultimately lost for good.
